title: Deep Koopman Observer-based Robust Model Predictive Control against Learned-model Mismatch and External Disturbances
abstract: This study presents a deep Koopman observer based model predictive control (MPC) framework for accurate trajectory tracking in robotic manipulators, addressing the learned-model mismatch between the finite-dimensional Koopman predictor and the actual robot dynamics. To estimate the mismatch and external disturbances, deep Koopman observer is proposed, and the estimates are incorporated into the finite horizon prediction of the MPC. To guarantee the tracking-error stability of the proposed MPC, a finite-step relaxed control Lyapunov function constraint is proposed. Real-robot experiments under various fixed payloads demonstrate a reduction in root mean square error of up to 98.0% over conventional Koopman based MPC frameworks.

title: Learning-Free Door-Opening Direction Estimation for Autonomous Wheelchairs Using a Single 360-Degree Camera
abstract: Autonomous wheelchairs have been deployed in airports, hospitals, and similar environments; however, their mobility is still limited because they cannot open or pass through standard doors other than automated ones. To navigate standard doors autonomously, a wheelchair must detect the door area, the door handle position, and the door-opening direction (left or right). Conventional approaches use onboard camera images and deep learning–based object detection to classify these elements into three classes: right-opening doors, left-opening doors, and door handles. However, this multi-class detection increases computational cost and is further constrained by the limited field of view of standard RGB cameras. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel method that equips a wheelchair with an omnidirectional camera. Using 360-degree images processed by YOLO11, the proposed method detects the door area and handle position, while the door-opening direction is determined without deep learning, based on the spatial relationship between the door and its handle. Experimental results show that, compared to the conventional method, the proposed approach improves performance, achieving a 2.5% increase in mAP50, a 5.4% increase in accuracy, and approximately a 5% improvement in F1- score across all detection classes. In addition, it achieves over 95% detection accuracy for objects within 4 meters and extends the detection range by 1 meter. These results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the conventional approach and is suitable for practical applications.

title: Procedurally generated high-fidelity 3D synthetic dataset for indoor building defect inspection
abstract: Indoor building defect inspection remains constrained by the lack of large, high-quality labeled datasets tailored to apartment interiors. During pre-occupancy inspection, defects must be identified reliably to support quality control and reduce rectification costs, yet manual inspection is time-consuming, subjective, and difficult to scale. Although deep learning has shown strong potential for automated defect detection, its practical deployment is limited by the scarcity of suitable training data. Existing public datasets are often focused on outdoor infrastructure, provide only low-resolution or classification-level labels, or lack the 3D spatial consistency needed for multi-view perception and embodied inspection systems. To address this gap, this project presents SynDefect3D, an open-source procedural framework for generating high-fidelity synthetic indoor defect data in navigable apartment environments. SynDefect3D is built on a 3D-native generation pipeline that procedurally synthesizes five common interior defect categories: crack, paint peel, spalling, paint bubble, and exposed wiring. Rather than modifying room-scale wall meshes directly, defects are generated as modular wall-attached assets, enabling fine morphological control while maintaining computational tractability. These defect instances are placed on apartment walls through constraint-guided rules that enforce realistic attachment and spacing conditions. The resulting scenes are assembled in sparse pre-occupancy apartment layouts and rendered with high-fidelity lighting, textures, and domain randomization to produce paired RGB images and pixel-accurate segmentation masks. The framework is fully seed-controlled, allowing for reproducible generation. Using this pipeline, the project releases a synthetic dataset of 27,680 annotated images at 1024 x 1024 resolution across 250 apartment room models. Each scene includes both room-level and defect-focused camera views, and five domain-randomization passes are applied to improve appearance diversity. The resulting dataset supports both semantic segmentation and object detection tasks. To validate dataset quality and usability, the project benchmarks multiple U-Net and YOLO models on the synthetic test split. Beyond synthetic benchmarks, the project also evaluates sim-to-real transfer. Models trained only on SynDefect3D demonstrate qualitative generalization to real apartment photographs despite domain shift. More importantly, when synthetic data is combined with a small manually annotated real dataset of 209 images, real-world object detection performance improves substantially, with mAP50:95 increasing by 359% relative to training on real data alone. Overall, SynDefect3D provides a scalable and reproducible foundation for training and benchmarking defect perception models, while also opening opportunities for future work in hybrid synthetic-real learning, embodied inspection, and robot-assisted building quality assessment.

title: When Search Becomes Memory: Accelerating Robot Design Discovery with Self-Evolving Skills
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as proposal generators for evolutionary robot design, yet most loops remain memoryless: simulator results shape the next population but are not preserved as reusable design knowledge. We present Auto-Robotist, a self-evolving LLM agent that distills morphology-search traces into an explicit natural-language skill library. Each skill stores a structural archetype, evidence-grounded positive and negative rules, and the evaluated designs that support them, making design memory inspectable rather than implicit in a population. During search, the agent retrieves skills to condition LLM edits of elite bodies while retaining a Genetic Algorithm (GA) mutation path for exploration; after evaluation, it updates the library through Add, Diagnose, and Merge. Across seven EvoGym tasks spanning locomotion, traversal, and object interaction, Auto-Robotist improves cold-start search and transfers learned skills to higher design spaces, where reference-conditioned transfer outperforms GA on every task. These results suggest that LLM agents can convert expensive physical evaluations into reusable, auditable design principles.

title: A Deterministic Ground Texture SLAM Simulator with Learned Ground Texture Fields
abstract: Ground texture localization and SLAM lack simulators that combine realistic imagery with a spatially consistent, revisitable world and controllable camera and trajectory conditions. We present a deterministic learned ground texture field that supports arbitrary physical-coordinate queries and renders user-specified trajectories and camera configurations with exact ground truth. We validate fields trained on four datasets and multiple hardware setups using texture comparisons, spatial-consistency tests, and matched real and simulated localization experiments. A real-photo mosaic reproduces most of the measured real–simulation gap, while tested camera and image effects do not, suggesting that observation-dependent appearance is a major challenge for ground texture localization. We then isolate camera-roll calibration error while holding the ground texture and robot trajectory fixed and find that small errors degrade visual odometry before GTBoW place recognition. Loop-closure correction improves trajectory error by $12.3times$ at $0.5^circ$ but provides no measurable benefit at $5^circ$, highlighting the importance of accurate camera extrinsic calibration for ground texture SLAM.

title: Deep Learning-Based Framework for Efficient Multigoal Shortest Path Planning in Indoor Environments
abstract: Connecting multiple destinations with the shortest overall path in an obstacle-rich indoor environment is a classic problem in robotic path planning. Established solutions, such as A*, ARA*, and RRT*, execute faster when given smaller input maps that exclude extraneous paths. However, removing such paths without losing the ground truth solution is challenging, because runtime-efficient approximations can yield detours. This work proposes a deep learning-based Search-Space Reduction Pipeline (SRP) that integrates a module called MazeNet to solve indoor navigation tasks with fast runtimes while maintaining accuracy. We transform the indoor environment into a graph representation, reducing the planning task into a graph-based optimization problem known as the Obstacle-Avoiding Rectilinear Steiner Minimum Tree (OARSMT). MazeNet takes compressed images derived from graph abstractions as inputs and uses a recurrent convolutional neural network (RCNN) trained to predict the shortest feasible path connecting all destinations. Within SRP, MazeNet’s output restricts the search space for classical planners. MazeNet solves more complex instances than those seen during training via recurrence with an integrated termination condition. We evaluate MazeNet's runtime and path-length performance using a variety of planning methods against both exact and approximate graph algorithms in simulations and, after fine-tuning, in real-life floor plans. MazeNet solves all these specific test cases with improved runtimes and no increase in path length. Physics simulation further supports MazeNet's feasibility in the tested floor plans, with no recorded collisions during the navigation tasks.

title: Classical HSV vs. Fine-Tuned YOLO11n for Stop-Sign Detection on F1TENTH/RoboRacer
abstract: We deploy two stop-sign detectors on an F1TENTH/RoboRacer autonomous racing vehicle (NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, Intel RealSense D435i): a classical HSV-based pipeline and a fine-tuned YOLO11n model. We compare both across seven standardized track scenarios covering baseline detection, distractor resistance, multi-sign sequencing, and partial occlusion. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first direct on-car comparison of classical and deep learning sign detectors on the F1TENTH/RoboRacer platform. We also contribute a reusable evaluation protocol designed to stress each failure mode independently. YOLO11n eliminates all three false positives produced by HSV (3 FP -> 0 FP) while matching HSV on every scenario where HSV succeeds. Specificity measures how well a detector ignores non-stop signs; YOLO11n achieves perfect specificity (1.00) versus HSV's 0.63, meaning HSV triggers unwanted stops on distractors such as YIELD and ROADWORK signs that share red coloring or similar geometry. Sensitivity measures how reliably a detector catches true stop signs; across 11 stop signs, YOLO11n correctly detects 9 (sensitivity 0.82) versus HSV's 8 (sensitivity 0.73), with both false negatives tracing to detector-agnostic limits: one cooldown lockout and one 2/3-occlusion failure shared by both, and one additional cooldown FN unique to HSV in S2. A 5.5 MB YOLO11n model at one-fifth frame rate on the Orin Nano therefore achieves higher specificity and higher sensitivity than classical CV. This work is a precursor to an ongoing multi-class extension targeting 14+ sign categories, including traffic lights, on the same platform.

title: Wire-Guided Mobile Robot for Multimodal Inspection of Long-Distance Belt Conveyors in Steel Plants
abstract: Long-distance belt conveyors in steel plants are critical infrastructure for bulk material handling, yet their inspection remains challenging due to extended operating ranges, elevated installation, and harsh environmental conditions including dust, moisture, and falling debris, idler bearing degradation, roll misalignment, belt tearing, material accumulation, and overheating of drive components can lead to severe downtime and, in coal transport lines, fire hazards. Existing inspection practices based on manual patrols or fixed sensing systems are limited in scalability, localization accuracy, and cost-effectiveness over plant-scale conveyor networks. This paper presents a wire-guided mobile robotic system for autonomous multimodal inspection of belt conveyors in steel plants. The proposed platform travels along fixed steel wires installed beside the conveyor and integrates a detachable sensing suite consisting of an omnidirectional microphone. an RGB camera, and a near-infrared thermal imaging camera. While traversing the inspection route, the robot acquires synchronized acoustic, visual and thermal data for detecting abnormal idler behavior, belt surface damage, drive-unit overheating, smoke or fire symptoms, and excessive material spillage around guide rollers. Precise fault localization is achieved using encoder-based position tracking during robot motion. To enable reliable deployment in outdoor bulk-material environments, the system incorporates a mechanically stable wire-driven mobility structure, optional dual-wire support for enhanced safety under wind disturbance, and a docking station for wireless charging and standby operation. The collected multimodal data are segmented in temporal or frame-based units and processed by a deep-learning-based diagnostic framework that classifies conveyor conditions and issues graded alarms. To reduce plant-wide communication burden, only inference outputs and event-level information are transmitted to the control room. To proposed approach offers a practical alternative to dense installation of fixed monitoring devices by combining mobility, multimodal perception, and onboard intelligent diagnosis in a single inspection platform. It is expected to improve maintenance efficiency, enable early fault detection, reduce fire risk, and enhance the operational safety and reliability of long-distance conveyor systems in steel manufacturing environments.

title: Evacuation Planning for Multiple Drone Failures in Drone Light Shows
abstract: Drone light shows have emerged as a popular form of entertainment in recent years. However, several high-profile incidents involving large-scale drone failures---where multiple drones simultaneously fall from the sky---have raised safety and reliability concerns. To ensure robustness, we propose a drone evacuation algorithm specifically designed for multiple drone failures in drone light shows, aimed at mitigating the risk of cascading collisions by parking at safe locations during drone-dropping incidents. Our algorithm integrates a trajectory prediction to predict the trajectories of failing drones and employs anytime rapidly-exploring random trees algorithms to compute near-optimal evacuation paths that minimize the likelihood of surviving drones being hit by fallen drones. Our experiments showed that our approach can greatly increase the robustness of a multi-drone system by leveraging deep learning to predict the trajectories of fallen drones.

title: Cache-Age-Aware Reuse of VLM Representations for Efficient VLA Inference
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but they typically execute a large Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbone for every action chunk, which introduces significant inference latency. We propose reusing the internal representation of the VLM across multiple action chunks, reducing the VLM execution frequency to once every K chunks. The Action Expert is explicitly conditioned on a reuse-stage embedding that indicates how outdated the cached VLM representation is, and a frozen lightweight vision transformer supplies up-to-date visual features for every action chunk through cross attention, compensating for short-term visual changes such as object displacement and robot motion. On the LIBERO benchmark, a single trained model allows the reuse period K to be varied at inference time: the success rate degrades gracefully from 97.0% (K=1) to 78.3% (K=5), whereas a baseline trained without the reuse-stage conditioning drops to 73.6% even at K=1 and below 58% for K>=2. The reuse reduces the mean per-chunk latency on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 from 498 ms (K=1) to 355 ms (K=3) and 322 ms (K=5), corresponding to speedups of 1.40x and 1.55x, so the reuse period can be selected according to the latency budget of the target platform without retraining.

title: Anomaly Detection under Moving Viewpoints Using World Coordinate Features
abstract: Recently, labor shortage in retail stores is becoming severe, and the automation of product arrangement by robot is expected. Because there are countless states of products to be arranged, we defined them as anomaly products. We have developed a robot that detects them using an anomaly detection Neural Network (NN). However, conventional anomaly detection NNs are mainly designed for a fixed camera, making it difficult to detect multiple kinds of products over a wide area while moving. In this study, we focus on the world coordinates of products, which are independent of camera motion. We propose a novel anomaly detection NN using features extracted from an autoencoder that reconstructs the world coordinates. Experimental results showed that our method achieved a detection rate of 87.0 %, which was 12.6 points higher than a representative method for fixed cameras. In addition, a mobile robot equipped with our method successfully removed 85 % of anomaly products from a shelf.

title: Glance Globally, Restore Locally: Lightweight Tiled Dehazing of Native 4K Images for Robotic Vision
abstract: Unmanned robots must operate through sea fog and fire smoke, where camera-based perception degrades and onboard compute is limited. Native ultra-high-definition (UHD) dehazing must recover fine detail at 3840x2160, yet full-image processing with large networks is computation- and memory-heavy, while independent tile processing loses global haze, illumination, and color context. We present FLR-TileDehaze, a compact CNN-only method coupling a full-image low-resolution (FLR) guidance branch with overlapping high-resolution tile restoration, in two operating points: Lite (22.6K parameters) and Quality (33.6K; adds a global refinement and a low-resolution residual field). On a fixed local 1,562-image 4KID test split, Lite and Quality reach 17.76/17.88 dB PSNR, Quality improving all five evaluated metrics over Lite. On an RTX 3090, a frozen mixed-precision backend delivers 39-41 FPS native-4K model-path throughput without retraining, within 0.002 dB of FP32 validation PSNR. Among methods exceeding 30 FPS under this same-split protocol, our configurations achieve the highest PSNR, motivating resource-efficient preprocessing for high-resolution robotic vision.

title: Next Best View Selection for Object Pose Estimation based on Predicted Images at Next Views
abstract: Automating product display in retail stores requires accurate object pose estimation. Object pose is generally estimated using RGB-D cameras. However, simple-shaped products often lack sufficient visual information for accurate pose estimation from a single viewpoint. Therefore, active vision approaches improve pose estimation accuracy by moving the camera based on Next-Best-View (NBV) selection. However, conventional state-of-the-art methods rely on human-defined hypotheses that do not necessarily suit the characteristics of pose estimation neural networks. In this paper, we propose a novel NBV selection method based on a new metric called “pseudo-confidence.” Our method selects the next viewpoint based on the output of the pose estimation neural network itself. Before moving the camera, our method predicts the images that could be captured from candidate next viewpoints. By inputting these predicted images into the pose estimation neural network, we compute the pseudo-confidence for each candidate viewpoint. The next viewpoint is selected by maximizing this pseudo-confidence. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms conventional methods, improving the average pose estimation accuracy by 2.7 points. Furthermore, a robot equipped with our method successfully displayed 84.2% of products, achieving a 14.0-point improvement over the previous state-of-the-art method.

title: Intelligent Wheelchair Navigation Along Braille Blocks via Omnidirectional Vision and External Joystick Actuation
abstract: In countries such as Japan, where the population is rapidly aging, the burden on caregivers and nurses in nursing homes and hospitals is increasing. One of their main burdens is to assist in moving the patient/caregiver. Many of them are wheelchair users, and accompanying them to their destinations is burdensome. Electric wheelchairs have been developed as a way to reduce the burden, but they require the passenger to operate the wheelchair himself/herself, which places a burden on the wheelchair user. To solve these problems, we propose an all-sky camera mounted on an electric wheelchair to automatically detect Braille blocks in all directions by machine learning, and propose a traveling assistance system that automatically runs the electric wheelchair along the detected Braille blocks. First, Braille blocks are detected using You Only Look Once version5 (YOLOv5) on images obtained from a 360-degree camera. Then, the system determines the direction of travel based on the Braille block detection results. Next, the distance between the wheelchair and the Braille block is estimated. For the distance estimation, we propose a new method based on the equidistant projection method used to generate a 360-degree camera image. Based on this information, the joystick is operated to keep the wheelchair at a certain distance along the Braille blocks to assist the wheelchair in traveling. In this study, a new mechanism that can be installed in any type of electric wheelchair was developed to operate the joystick. In the verification experiment, the detection accuracy of Braille blocks in indoor and outdoor environments was 97.3%, the accuracy of determining the direction of travel was 100%, and the average error in measuring the distance between the wheelchair and Braille blocks was 0.15m. The proposed system was validated by the above algorithm, which enabled the wheelchair to run automatically.

title: CVLAMP: Compliant Vision Language Action Movement Primitives
abstract: We present Compliant Vision-Language-Action Movement Primitives (CVLAMP), a closed-loop framework for contact-rich dual-arm manipulation. CVLAMP conditions a VLA backbone on images, language, Cartesian state, and force history, decoding a compact Cartesian motion primitive in place of a dense action chunk. Each primitive couples a Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) pose rollout with shared-phase wrench and gripper profiles, executed by a phase-governed controller that can run, slow, hold, or abort from real-time feedback. The architecture extends a pretrained π0.5 flow-matching VLA with cross-attention-fused state and force encoders, trained with a composite regression, rollout-consistency, and mode-classification objective via staged, single-GPU LoRA adaptation of the released checkpoint. In simulation, the model localizes the goal object from vision alone with a mean 2D position error of approximately 5.5 cm on held-out, previously unseen object positions, and the closed-loop system reliably approaches and grasps the target object; full task completion and real-robot deployment are ongoing work.

title: Toward Conversational VLMs: A Pilot Taxonomy of Robot Response Decisions from Wizard-of-Oz Assistive Interaction
abstract: Robots that follow natural-language instructions in everyday indoor environments must act on incomplete human utterances. Instructions often omit essential information, such as the identity of an out-of-view object, an intended destination, or the user's goal. Existing datasets contain little real-world situated dialogue and provide few practice-grounded criteria for deciding when a robot should act, confirm, clarify, or refuse. We retrospectively analyze a pilot Wizard-of-Oz study in which five participants performed everyday indoor tasks, including door opening, drawer opening, feeding, drinking, and cleaning, with a wheelchair-mounted mobile manipulator while the wizard responded without a prescribed asking policy. This preserved authentic user behavior but produced inconsistent robot-side decisions, motivating an explicit decision scheme. From 40 episodes, we derive a two-level taxonomy of six response modes (ANSWER, REPORT_DONE, REFUSE, CONFIRM, CLARIFY, ACT) and four ambiguity types (intent, referential, spatial, intelligibility). Two human annotators and an AI annotator applied the scheme to the pilot data. Clean-label rates were 91% and 89%, and Cohen's kappa ranged from 0.72 to 0.96 across decision-point, mode, and ambiguity levels for both human-human and human-AI comparisons. Fine-tuning LLaVA-1.6-7B on taxonomy-derived labels for ACT and CLARIFY indicates the feasibility of training vision language models using annotations from our taxonomy. Remaining boundary cases in decision-point identification and REPORT_DONE motivate a constrained protocol for standardized dialogue collection.

title: CR-VSCP: Evidence-Gated VLM Semantic Constraints for Autonomous Driving with Reduced HD Map Dependency
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide traffic semantics that are difficult to encode geometrically, but se- mantically plausible outputs may still be physically inconsis- tent. In this paper, we propose the Coarse-Route-guided VLM Semantic Constraint Planner (CR-VSCP), which treats VLM outputs as event hypotheses rather than motion commands. Candidate trajectories first pass VLM-independent feasibility checks for collision avoidance, drivable-area compliance, and vehicle-dynamics constraints. A VLM event can affect candidate ranking only after Evidence-Gated Verification (EVG) confirms route consistency and independent physical evidence. On 12,147 NAVSIM navtest frames, the complete planner achieves a PDM Score (PDMS) of 0.810. On held-out semantic-event data, EVG increases stop/yield precision from 15% to 47–57% and reduces false stops from 26% to 6%. A log-clustered bootstrap over 57 driving logs further shows that direct lateral VLM intervention significantly degrades planning performance. These results sup- port a division of responsibility in which VLMs interpret non- geometric driving semantics while an explicit planner retains authority over trajectory geometry and hard safety constraints.

title: Query-gated Dual-View Fusion for Submillimeter-Precision CNC Lathe Manipulation
abstract: Loading a ring-shaped metal workpiece into a CNC lathe chuck requires submillimeter alignment: even a small visual error can cause the final insertion to fail. The robot must first establish the global spatial relationship between the workpiece and the chuck, and then resolve fine workpiece--chuck geometry near contact. A head camera provides the global spatial location of the workpiece, whereas a wrist camera resolves the fine alignment between the workpiece and the chuck; therefore, the relative importance of the two views varies across different stages of the task. We present a query-gated dual-view policy that preserves dense patch tokens from a frozen vision encoder, retrieves task-relevant evidence independently from each view, and adaptively fuses the retrieved features at the query and channel levels. The fused visual representations, together with proprioceptive history, condition a diffusion decoder that predicts future action chunks. Trained on 600 real-robot trajectories, the policy achieves 100% insertion success in the nominal setting (50/50 trials). It further succeeds in 71/100 trials under positional perturbations of up to 20 mm and in 67/100 trials under rotational perturbations of up to $4^circ$. These preliminary results suggest that explicitly routing complementary global and local visual evidence is a promising interface for precision visuomotor control.

title: A Two-Stage Deep Learning Framework for In-Situ Soil Property Estimation from Multivariate Sensor Sequence
abstract: Reliable soil fertility measurement is essential for precision agriculture, but electrochemical sensor measurements are often affected by measurement noise and environmental disturbances. This paper proposes a two-stage deep learning framework for soil fertility estimation. A multi-head attention based LSTM network is first employed to denoise multivariate electrochemical sensor data, followed by a modernTCN for soil NO− 3 estimation. The experimental results indicate that the proposed framework captures the overall temporal variability of electrochemical sensor measurements, for real-time soil fertility estimation.

title: Human-guided RL-based Cooperative Manipulation for Dual-arm Agricultural Robots
abstract: This study proposes a human-guided RL-based cooperative manipulation method for dual-arm agricultural robots performing various farming tasks in complex environments. By combining imitation learning and reinforcement learning, the proposed method enables the system to learn efficient and stable manipulation strategies while reducing reliance on manually designed control rules. First, the system learns human behaviors related to farming tasks through behavior cloning (BC), and then refines the learned policy using the proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm to enhance robustness and adaptability across diverse agricultural environments. This enables the system to mimic complex dual arm cooperative behaviors, such as performing a primary task with one arm while removing obstacles with the other, allowing efficient operation even in complex and irregular environments. Through this study, agricultural robots are expected to perform tasks in a human-like manner across complex and diverse agricultural environments.

title: Vision-Language Robotic Instrument Handover for Operation
abstract: Instrument handover is one of the most repetitive and timing-sensitive tasks in an operating room, and it degrades with staff fatigue. We present a vision-language prototype that turns a spoken instrument request into a physical handover on a bench that mimics an operating room. Recognition runs a three-stage cascade: a local prototype classifier matches a whole utterance, SenseVoice-Small transcription is matched against an instrument lexicon and a per-surgeon alias table, and acoustic template matching acts as a fallback. A short enrollment mode adapts the recognizer to each surgeon in Mandarin, Cantonese, or English. An OpenPI vision-language-action model, fine-tuned on a surgical-instrument dataset, returns the target region for six instrument classes, and the arm replays a per-instrument trajectory. Emergency abort, exit, and a task cooldown sit outside every learned module. Across 360 end-to-end trials, the prototype completed 90.28% of handovers, with 4.719 s mean voice response and 14.688 s mean delivery.

title: Monocular Indoor Navigation with Visual–Floor-Plan Alignment and a Reactive RL Policy
abstract: We present an indoor navigation framework that combines visual–floor-plan alignment, implemented through cross-modal grounding, with a reactive reinforcement-learning (RL) policy. The only exteroceptive sensor is a monocular RGB camera; a human-oriented 2D floor plan provides the global spatial reference. The alignment module provides a grounded pose that yields the relative goal distance and bearing; the policy generates local motion from the current segmented image. We compare two configurations that share the same PPO policy and differ in the source of this relative goal. On fixed Route 1, in a simulated area excluded from training, Proposed completed 20/20 repeated trials and Odometry + PPO 13/20; a LiDAR-based AMCL + Nav2 reference also completed 20/20. Successful example trajectories were obtained on Routes 2 and 3 as qualitative evidence only. Grounded-pose trajectories show visible offsets near symmetric branches, which did not prevent the robot from reaching the goal.

title: Zero-Shot Transfer of a Map-Free Reinforcement Learning Navigation Policy from a Differential-Drive Robot to a Quadruped Robot
abstract: A map-free deep reinforcement learning (DRL) navigation policy, trained entirely in simulation for a differential-drive robot, is transferred zero-shot to a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot, with no additional training or fine-tuning on the new platform. Semantic segmentation bridges the visual gap between simulation and reality by generating binary visual observations consistent with those used during training, while self-localization is provided by a stereo visual-inertial odometry (VIO) pipeline that requires no prior map or LiDAR. Real-world experiments in an indoor corridor demonstrate stable, long-distance autonomous navigation, confirming that a navigation policy learned for a differential-drive robot transfers zero-shot to a quadruped platform.

title: Encoder-Free Hexapod Dead Reckoning on Sand Using Learned Inertial Correction
abstract: For inexpensive legged robots traversing remote natural terrain, minimal-sensing localization strongly affects autonomous range and search efficiency. Although proprioceptive sensors such as inertial measurement units (IMU) are compact and widely used on robotic platforms, direct integration of noisy inertial measurements causes small sensor errors to propagate into large pose estimation errors, limiting their use as independent dead reckoning sensors. In this work, we address drift in encoder-free dead reckoning by combining body-frame acceleration profiles from a compact multi-IMU array with commanded motion parameters in a convolutional neural network (CNN) bias estimator. The estimator predicts the difference between commanded and realized platform displacement, without using joint encoders or explicit terrain labels. In outdoor local search experiments with an encoder-free hexapod robot, the proposed approach reduces mean dead reckoning drift by approximately 41% on grass and 59% on sand relative to an idealized commanded-kinematics baseline. These results indicate that a platform-specific dataset collected in controlled indoor terrains improves outdoor dead reckoning performance, even when the deployment terrain is not fully represented in the training dataset. This method provides a low-cost, compact proprioceptive drift reduction method for minimally instrumented legged robots when exteroceptive localization is unavailable due to cost or environmental conditions. We expect this approach to be helpful in developing future low-cost robots for scrambling across extraterrestrial, underwater, or underground granular media where leg slip is both common and hard to predict.

title: Weld-PICA: Traceable and Uncertainty-Aware Human-in-the-Loop Evidence for GMAW Weld Inspection
abstract: End-to-end AI systems increasingly combine perception and language models to turn sensor data into human-facing assessments. Their outputs, however, are difficult to review when confidence scores are detached from source evidence, generated descriptions contain unsupported details, or uncertainty from different modules is collapsed into one value. We present Weld-PICA, a human-in-the-loop framework that converts object detections into source-linked, crop-grounded evidence records with explicit uncertainty and bounded interaction. Gas metal arc welding (GMAW) defect inspection provides the current case study, but the design applies more broadly to detection-plus-vision-language workflows in which a person retains decision authority. The offline prototype links YOLOv7 detections, padded crops, local vision-language observations, and stable finding identifiers. We describe the interaction model and a planned evaluation spanning detection, evidence grounding, and ProbVLM-style semantic uncertainty.

title: A Wearable Hand Exoskeleton with ML-Based Proportional Grip Force Control from EMG
abstract: Most wrist and hand exoskeletons are designed for clinical rehabilitation, leaving continuous, everyday grip assistance largely unaddressed. We present an open-source, tendon-driven hand exoskeleton with independently actuated 3-DOF thumb control and machine-learning-based proportional grip force control from surface electromyography (sEMG). The system enables continuous, muscle-driven modulation of grip strength rather than discrete gesture classification or threshold-gated actuation. An 8-channel, 500 Hz sEMG armband provides a 107-dimensional feature set comprising time-domain, frequency-domain, and cross-channel features to a machine learning regression model that estimates grip force in real time. Four regression architectures, XGBoost, support vector regression, random forest, and gradient boosting, were benchmarked using 5-fold cross-validation grouped by calibration trial to prevent window-level data leakage. XGBoost matched the highest offline accuracy (R² = 0.962) while training 6-7 times faster than random forest and gradient boosting, facilitating rapid per-user recalibration. Across 10 able-bodied participants, the deployed controller achieved real-time filtered performance of R² = 0.918 (NRMSE = 8.2%, r = 0.976) against synchronously measured ground-truth grip force, with predictions leading measured force by a mean of 173 ms. In a separate pilot assessment, the exoskeleton was evaluated on an individual with spinal cord injury (SCI), comparing hand range of motion with and without device assistance; the exoskeleton increased the participant's overall hand range of motion from 12.2% to 60.8% of the unimpaired reference range. Independently, the device's own actuation was characterized to deliver up to 13 N of grip force (peak 17 N) and 3.3 N of pinch force (peak 4.7 N) with no user effort applied. Representative trials illustrate the underlying signal quality: for the top-performing able-bodied participant, median-filtered predictions closely tracked measured force (R² = 0.983), while for the SCI participant, raw predictions were visibly noisier before the 7-window median filter recovered the underlying force trajectory (R² improving from 0.682 to 0.822). These results demonstrate that the proposed proportional sEMG control framework can be reliably calibrated and deployed across a heterogeneous multi-user cohort while maintaining accurate real-time grip force estimation. The SCI pilot further provides preliminary evidence of functional benefit, supporting the feasibility of continuous, EMG-driven proportional control for everyday assistive hand exoskeletons beyond the rehabilitation clinic.

title: Do Rigid-Body Simulators Dream of Soft Robots? Learning Contact-Rich Manipulation for Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots
abstract: Learning contact-rich, whole-body manipulation for soft continuum robots is held back by the lack of simulation infrastructure that has accelerated rigid-robot manipulation. Existing soft robot simulators are physically grounded but lack the contact handling, actuation support, or learning integration needed for contact-rich manipulation; rigid-body approximations offer these capabilities but sacrifice physical grounding. We bridge this gap for tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) by deriving a continuum-mechanics-informed discretization that places the soft robot natively inside MuJoCo, unifying tendon forces, body contact, and dynamics in a single physics pipeline. We validate the simulator against a Cosserat rod reference (static and dynamic) and real TDCR hardware. We then train state-based imitation learning policies via teleoperation in simulation and deploy them zero-shot to a physical 3-segment TDCR on a 7-DoF Franka arm across two contact-rich manipulation tasks. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of sim-to-real transfer for contact-rich manipulation with continuum robots.

title: From Conversation to Execution: Learning through instruction and dialog for Robots in Safety-Critical Environments.
abstract: Teaching robots new procedural tasks remains a persistent challenge. Manual programming requires engineering effort for every task, learning from demonstration requires many physical examples, and policies trained on large datasets are opaque and difficult to verify, a serious limitation in safety-critical settings. We address this challenge with dialog-based script learning grounded entirely in symbolic, interpreted knowledge. Scripts describe complex events with component subevents, and ontologically grounded agents use them to represent the procedural knowledge necessary to execute complex tasks. In our system, an agent configured in an ontologically grounded cognitive architecture operates within HARMONIC, a cognitive robotic architecture, and learns a complete, executable task script from a single natural-language walkthrough given by a human teammate, with no training data, no reward tuning, and no statistical approximation of meaning. The teammate's utterances are translated into ontologically grounded meaning representations over which all reasoning is carried out. The learning procedure is itself encoded declaratively as a metascript in the agent's ontology, describing the sequence of events the agent undertakes when learning. This includes recognizing a teaching intent, selecting a learning target, normalizing and ordering the event sequence, extracting preconditions, and incorporating the finished script and associated lexicon entries into the agent's knowledge resources, at which point it is immediately executable. The approach is domain-independent, operating over a large lexicon and ontology rather than a narrow vocabulary, and every stage of learning and every piece of learned knowledge can be read, checked, and corrected by a human, a property valuable for safety-critical human-robot teaming. We demonstrate the metascript by tracing how a robot learns to replace a fuse through dialog with a human partner and then executes the task in a simulated ship engine room.

title: Enhancing the Evaluation of Vision-Language Models for Video Understanding
abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) extend Large Language Models (LLMs) using visual encoders and provide understanding about images and videos. Evaluating VLMs is necessary to improve the confidence of their inference. In this work, we developed an enhanced question and answer dataset that will be used to evaluate VLMs. This was done by using a ground truth human annotated dataset, where a more diverse dataset was generated using the NVIDIA-Nemotron 3.

title: PC-VLA: A Sub-Million Parameter Predictive-Coding Policy for Language-Conditioned Robot Manipulation
abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance in robotic manipulation, but often rely on billions of parameters and large-scale robot pretraining. We introduce PC-VLA, a compact predictive-coding policy for language-conditioned robot manipulation that achieves competitive performance without large-scale robot pretraining. PC-VLA combines a frozen visual-language frontend with a lightweight 0.676M-parameter trainable recurrent policy. The recurrent hierarchy jointly predicts visual observations, proprioceptive states, and actions, while online error regression continuously updates the internal latent trajectory using sensory prediction errors. Hierarchical recurrent layers operating at different time scales capture both slow task-level structure and fast motor dynamics. We evaluate PC-VLA on LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-Object using 14 independently trained seeds and 50 rollouts per task. PC-VLA achieves an average success rate of 86.8%, while substantially outperforming parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM behavior-cloning baselines. Ablation studies further show that hierarchical temporal structure and online latent-state inference are critical to performance. These results suggest that predictive and hierarchical architectures with online inference provide a parameter-efficient alternative to scaling model size and robot pretraining data for language-conditioned robot manipulation.

title: Leveraging Augmented Reality to Bridge the Sim2Real Gap in Robotic Movement Visualization
abstract: This research focuses on enhancing the visualization of planning and executing robot movement in an intuitive and understandable way for humans, aiming to contribute a more coherent form of communication for human-robot interaction and bridge the gap between simulation to reality by bringing simulation overlayed into reality. We aim to develop a web-based interface that utilizes augmented reality (AR) for a Meta Quest headset application. We aim to provide users with comprehensible information regarding the robot's plan and projected movements to complete typical household chores. We describe our approach of connecting out an external camera device to our robotic system, implementing object detection and localization, and visualizing planned robot movements in preparation for execution through our web-based interface. Using our interface, the user is presented with overlayed trajectory information of the movement path that the robot plans to execute from an external point of view other than the robot's to allow for more environmental awareness. This work has great potential impact on furthering human-robot interaction, especially in shared tasks, for domestic robots by improving robot-to-user communication.

title: Exploring Soft Continuum Robot Capabilities Through Control Theory and Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Soft continuum robots are highly underactuated and redundant, which makes control difficult due to limited control authority and weak stability guarantees. In this work, we show empirically that even for a simple trajectory-tracking task, PD- and Quadratic Program(QP)-PD-based task-space controllers can fail as the level of underactuation increases: without an inherent stability and convergence guarantee, these methods can map a desired task-space acceleration onto an infeasible joint-space acceleration. To actively enforce stability in the task-space error dynamics while respecting actuator constraints, we introduce a Soft Inverse Dynamics Control Lyapunov Function-based Quadratic Program (Soft ID-CLF_x0002_QP) tailored to highly underactuated soft robots. Experimental results demonstrate superior set-point and trajectory-tracking accuracy alongside consistent Lyapunov convergence compared to baseline methods. Furthermore, to handle contact-rich tasks where soft robot physics are difficult to model, such as object manipulation, we deploy an LSTM-based Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement learning policy in a partially observable setting. Preliminary simulation and sim_x0002_to-real hardware experiments show high-quality sweeping and grasping performance.

title: Behavior is a Language for Cross-Embodiment Control
abstract: Behavior cloning (BC) models demonstrations as a sequence prediction problem often conditioned on a goal state, to reap the stability and performance benefits of supervised learning. Learning robot affordances by observing humans is generally a good idea since humans often act in near-optimal ways. However, robotic agents historically suffer from an embodiment problem. That is, an algorithm cannot simultaneously control all robotic systems; it becomes overfitted to the robot hardware, or embodiment, used in training. This creates additional challenges when learning from human experience as humans and robots have different bodies. This work presents BeLa, a flexible model that learns robot behavior from human examples. BeLa's design is based on the Perciever-IO transformer~cite{perceiverio}. This allows the model to attend to varying input/output sizes without adjustments. We hypothesize that this (1) helps to facilitate model reuse and (2) allows the model to benefit from broader pretraining than could be done with VLA that use action heads.

title: Toward Vision-Guided Terrain-Adaptive Locomotion in a Sea Turtle-Inspired Robot
abstract: Autonomous terrain-adaptive locomotion in low- profile, bio-inspired robots relies on onboard perception, yet near- ground clearance introduces severe optical bottlenecks. While sensor placement and viewpoint selection are well studied in mobile robotics, prior work largely focuses on taller quadrupeds, humanoids, and rovers rather than low-profile crawlers. As a result, grazing-angle views and texture foreshortening remain challenging for near-ground terrain sensing. This work presents an onboard vision-based terrain-recognition framework for a sea turtle-inspired robot. A MobileNetV2 classifier is trained on GTOS-Mobile imagery remapped into seven locomotion-relevant classes and adapted to the robot-camera domain using session- separated fine-tuning. Aspect-ratio-preserving letterboxing re- tains the complete camera field of view. The classifier is deployed on a Raspberry Pi 5 and integrated with the robot’s Central Pattern Generator (CPG) architecture, using terrain estimates to inform locomotion-mode selection. On 710 robot images from nine held-out sessions, fine-tuning increased accuracy from 52.39% to 83.10% and macro F1-score from 46.78% to 83.11%. Remaining errors were concentrated at the sand–solid-ground boundary, with 104 of 154 solid-ground images classified as sand. These results validate the hardware perception-to-CPG interface and motivate improved camera placement for closed-loop, vision- triggered gait adaptation.

title: Slow Thinking, Fast Safe Control: A Modular Alternative to End-to-End Vision-Language-Action
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated impressive semantic generalization for robotic manipulation, but they typically couple perception, reasoning, and low-level action prediction within a single learned policy [1,2]. This makes it difficult to impose explicit runtime safety constraints and creates a mismatch between the relatively slow rate of vision-language reasoning and the fast feedback required for safety-critical control. Sampling-based controllers such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control [3] and related approaches, such as Ensemble Kalman Inversion [4], provide fast closed-loop optimization but require that objectives, priors, and constraints be specified. Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide an explicit mechanism for runtime safety enforcement [5], yet do not determine task intent or how the robot should recover when a nominal action becomes unsafe. We present Slow Thinking, Fast Safe Control, a modular architecture that separates semantic reasoning, dynamic control, and runtime safety across complementary time scales. A vision-language model reasons over language instructions and multi-view visual observations to identify task-relevant objects, semantic constraints, subgoals, and route information. These outputs are compiled into objectives for an MPPI controller, which generates fast closed-loop actions, while a CBF layer projects nominal actions onto a constraint-satisfying set using robot-, obstacle-, and language-conditioned safety constraints. We evaluate the approach in MuJoCo on six manipulation challenges: obstacle pick-and-place, dynamic-obstacle transport, narrow-passage carrying, semantic keep-out, blocked-path recovery, and occluded-clutter retrieval. We compare SmolVLA, SmolVLA-CBF, and our VLM-MPPI-CBF architecture. SmolVLA uses a 450M-parameter policy with 99.9M fine-tuned parameters, trained on 128 demonstrations for 20k steps, while our method uses a frozen 3.75B-parameter Qwen2.5-VL model for semantic reasoning. In preliminary experiments, VLM-MPPI-CBF achieves 70% safe task success, compared with 13% for SmolVLA and 9% for SmolVLA-CBF. Our method exceeds 78% task success on five of six tasks and achieves 28% on the hardest task. These results suggest that explicit safety filtering alone cannot compensate for weak task execution, while separating semantic reasoning, fast model-based control, and runtime safety provides a promising direction for safer language-conditioned manipulation. References [1] Zitkovich et al., RT-2, CoRL 2023. [2] Kim et al., OpenVLA, CoRL 2025. [3] Williams et al., MPPI, IEEE TRO 2017. [4] Khalil et al., ADMM-EKI, IEEE LCSS 2026. [5] Ames et al., CBF-QP, IEEE TAC 2017.

title: Learning Differentiable Control Barrier Functions for Real-Time Safe Autonomy
abstract: This work introduces a learning-based approach for the numerical construction of control barrier functions (CBFs). The approach leverages the dynamic backup CBF framework to compute the CBF values over a given mesh. The collected data is then used to train a neural network that approximates both the CBF and its gradient. It is shown that tigtening the constraints with a safety margin can mitigate approximation errors at the safety boundary, suggesting a viable method of constructing computationally lightweight safe controllers for real-time robotic systems.

title: Gaze-Aware VLMs for Object Grounding in Human-Robot Interaction
abstract: In embodied human-robot interaction, people often refer to objects with underspecified language and behavioral cues such as gaze, for example saying ""clean that"" while looking at a vase. Vision-language models (VLMs) can read such behavior from images but cannot directly use the precise gaze direction a robot's sensors record. We study how to feed gaze directly into a VLM's input for object grounding, in three stages. Because the source interaction data contain no images, we first reconstruct the scenes in a virtual environment and render them from user, robot, and distributed viewpoints, and we train a gaze-alignment model that predicts when the user is attending to the target. Stage 1 then compares design choices in a fully crossed experiment: which camera view to use, whether to keep all frames or only the single predicted target-attended frame, and how to inject gaze (none, a visible marker on the frame, or patch-level feature weighting). Task-specific adaptation mattered most: the fine-tuned model outperformed both its untuned base and GPT-4o on target-related questions, and keeping the whole frame sequence beat using one frame. Gaze was not uniformly useful, since drawing it on every frame can hide the object and reduce accuracy on object type, color, and shape. Stage 2 therefore adopts a hybrid design that shows the gaze marker only on the predicted target-attended frame and leaves the rest of the clip untouched; it was the most balanced across question types, and no alternative significantly outperformed it. In Stage 3, a model adapted only on the virtual data improved on instructions collected in a real office, most clearly for relative position, which suggests that virtual reconstruction is a practical way to gather behavior-grounded interaction data.

title: Learning Expressive Humanoid Locomotion from Monocular Runway Videos for Robot Fashion Shows
abstract: Runway walking requires coordinated control of posture, stride, foot placement, and whole-body motion to effectively present clothing and convey a distinctive style. However, humanoid robots used in fashion shows typically rely on locomotion policies optimized primarily for stability and walking speed, limiting their ability to reproduce expressive, human-like runway motions. In this work, we present an end-to-end framework that transforms monocular runway videos into deployable humanoid locomotion policies through motion recovery, robot retargeting, motion correction, policy training, simulation-based evaluation, and physical deployment. We evaluate the proposed framework on the Booster K1 humanoid robot using runway-style catwalk motions. The learned policy completed every physical trial without falling, while reproducing the characteristic narrow foot placement and coordinated movement of the legs, torso, and arms. The results demonstrate that our proposed training framework enables the Booster K1 to perform stable and expressive catwalk motions, highlighting its potential for humanoid robotic applications in fashion shows and other performance-oriented scenarios.

title: DriveScene: A Comprehensive Video Dataset for Scenario Understanding, Generation, and Explanation in Autonomous Driving Research
abstract: Ensuring autonomous vehicles are trustworthy and transparent is crucial for safety and public trust, especially in high-stakes emergent scenarios. Existing driving datasets rarely capture safety-critical situations or provide the detailed annotations needed for explainable decision-making and human-centered scenario analysis. We introduce DriveScene, a large-scale ego-centric driving video dataset covering routine and emergent scenarios with annotations spanning scenario context, object-level grounding, and human-centered perception judgments. DriveScene contains 3,327 verified clips selected from 31,116 videos and aligns detailed scenario annotations with de-identified ratings and driving-related attributes collected from 408 participants. These rich annotations support important object identification, emergent video generation, explanation generation, and perceived-risk modeling.

title: Model Agnostic Agentic Framework for Long-Horizon Robotic Navigation and Planning
abstract: General purpose robots must reason over users natural language instructions while navigating diverse environments and be able to perform long-horizon tasks. Recent Vision Language Action (VLA) models attempt to address this challenge using end-to-end policies, but often require substantial task, environment and embodiment specific training and remain unstable when deployed in unseen environments. In this work we present a modular framework that decouples high level reasoning from low level motion control by combining a Vision Language Model (VLM) with classical robotic navigation approaches. In our framework, a VLM performs task planning, task breakdown, grounded tool usage, and monitoring, while RTAB-Map and Nav2 provide mapping, localization, dynamic collision avoidance, and trajectory execution without the need for environment specific fine-tuning. To bridge semantic reasoning with motion control, we introduce point navigation and map navigation tools that ground VLM predictions into 3D navigation goals using RGB camera images, depth maps, camera parameters, and TF transformations. Further more the framework incorporates a monitoring mechanism that enables the VLM to detect unsafe and unintended behaviors and trigger replanning during execution. We evaluate the framework across multiple benchmarks, including a Behavior-1K based benchmark and VLN-CE Habitat environment benchmark designed to assess the frameworks navigation capabilities. Results demonstrate the ability of our proposed approach to combine the high level planning ability of VLMs with the reliability of classical planners, enabling long-horizon navigation without retraining for individual environments or robot embodiments.

title: MABEL: An Open Anthropomorphic Mobile Bimanual Platform for Teleoperation and Learning
abstract: The race toward general-purpose manipulation has produced increasingly capable whole-body robots in industry, but these systems remain largely closed, while open academic platforms typically lack the dexterity, mobility and whole-body articulation needed to capture equally expressive demonstrations. This gap limits both reproducible hardware research and the diversity of data available for learning general-purpose manipulation. We present MABEL, an open anthropomorphic mobile bimanual platform for teleoperation and learning. MABEL combines a three-wheel holonomic swerve base, 0.635,m lift, actuated torso, 3-DOF neck, two 7-DOF arms and two 17-DOF tendon-driven hands, providing 56 functional degrees of freedom at a USD 9,670 bill of materials. Compared with the most articulated open bimanual platform in our survey, MABEL provides $3.5times$ the functional degrees of freedom at $0.69times$ the cost, with a fingertip workspace spanning 0.00 to 2.23,m. CAD, firmware, ROS,2 software and a MuJoCo simulation are released under the MIT license. MABEL supports whole-body teleoperation using an Apple Vision Pro and only head and wrist observations. Analytical retargeting separates head orientation from mobile-base motion without additional body trackers or mode switches, while a compliant whole-body controller incorporates a lift-dependent tip-over constraint. The same controller interface supports teleoperation and learned policies. We demonstrate MABEL on mobile pick-and-place, human handover and long-horizon navigation tasks, providing an open platform for reproducible research in dexterous mobile manipulation.

title: Biomechanical Design, Fabrication, and Reinforcement Learning–Based Control of a 9-DOF Upper-extremity Rehabilitation Exoskeleton
abstract: Upper-extremity rehabilitation robots require accurate multi-joint tracking despite friction, compliance, and parameter error, while maintaining anatomical alignment and bounded actuation. This work presents the design, fabrication, modeling, and real-time control of a modular nine-degree-of-freedom (9-DOF) left-arm exoskeleton spanning five shoulder-complex motions, elbow flexion-extension, forearm pronation-supination, and two wrist motions. A recurrent Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) policy performs state-dependent gain scheduling by generating 27 bounded, joint-specific coefficients for proportional, derivative, and integral-error feedback. The policy was trained with randomized trajectories and dynamics, frozen before deployment, and executed on an NI PXI real-time platform. Against computed-torque control (CTC) under the same nine-joint reference motion and actuator limits, it reduced mean position root-mean-square error from 1.986° to 1.325° (33.3%), worst-joint RMSE from 3.255° to 1.696° (47.9%), and maximum peak error from 5.89° to 2.29° (61.1%). Peak actuator demand was nearly identical (22.44 versus 22.41 N·m), with no saturation. Velocity RMSE increased slightly, so the evidence supports improved position tracking at comparable peak effort rather than universal dynamic superiority. Results are limited to robot-only laboratory testing; human-interaction safety, clinical efficacy, and patient-specific assistance remain to be established.
